entities.name: Marie Melchior Joseph Théodose de Lagrené
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marie Melchior Joseph Théodose de Lagrené (d. 1862-04-26) was a pivotal French legislator and diplomat whose mission to China in 1844 fundamentally reshaped Sino-French relations and solidified France's nascent imperial presence in East Asia. Dispatched by King Louis-Philippe amidst the aftermath of the First Opium War, Lagrené's objective was to secure for France commercial and religious privileges comparable to those extorted by Great Britain through the Treaty of Nanking. His diplomatic endeavors culminated in the Treaty of Whampoa, signed on October 24, 1844, a landmark agreement that marked France's entry into the system of "unequal treaties" imposed upon the weakening Qing Dynasty.

Lagrené's negotiations, conducted with the imperial commissioner Keying in Guangzhou, were meticulously detailed. The Treaty of Whampoa granted France extraterritoriality for its citizens in five treaty ports (Guangzhou, Fuzhou, Xiamen, Ningbo, and Shanghai), fixed customs tariffs, and, crucially, a most-favored-nation clause ensuring that any future concessions granted to other powers would automatically extend to France. A particularly significant provision, which Lagrené championed, was the formal toleration and protection of Catholic missionaries and their converts, marking a significant step in the re-establishment of Catholicism in China after centuries of sporadic persecution. This clause would have profound implications for future missionary activity and Western intervention.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Marie de Lagrené's negotiation of the Treaty of Whampoa in 1844 established France as a major Western power in China, significantly expanding European imperial reach and contributing to the systemic erosion of Qing sovereignty through the unequal treaty system. His work directly influenced subsequent Western diplomatic engagements and the trajectory of Sino-Western relations for over a century.

entities.summary: Marie Melchior Joseph Théodose de Lagrené was a French legislator and diplomat who played a crucial role in shaping the modern French state. Born on March 14, 1800, in Amiens, France, he rose to prominence during the Bourbon Restoration (1815-1830) as a key figure in the Chamber of Deputies. His efforts contributed significantly to the codification of French law and the establishment of the French civil service system. As a diplomat, de Lagrené served as ambassador to several European countries, including Austria and Prussia. His legacy extends beyond his own time, influencing the development of modern French politics and international relations. Notably, he was a vocal advocate for the rights of French citizens and worked tirelessly to promote social justice and equality. De Lagrené's contributions can be seen in the numerous laws and regulations he helped enact during his tenure, including the establishment of the French pension system and the promotion of education reform.
